paragraphs.heading: The 0 to 1 scale
paragraphs.text: Basic probability puts a number on how likely an event is. That number always sits between 0 and 1. The closer it is to 1, the more likely the event. You will often see the same number written as a percentage, running from 0% to 100%.

paragraphs.heading: Counting outcomes
paragraphs.text: Think of tossing a fair coin, one with no bias toward either side. There are only two possible results, heads and tails, and they are equally likely. Each therefore gets a probability of 1/2, the same as 0.5 or 50%. In the 1500s Gerolamo Cardano showed it works well to compare favourable outcomes with unfavourable ones. That idea means an event's probability is its favourable outcomes divided by all the possible outcomes.

paragraphs.heading: Probability as long-run frequency
paragraphs.text: One school, the objectivists, says a probability describes something real in the world. Its best-known form is frequentist probability. On this view, the probability of an outcome is how often it turns up if you repeat the experiment again and again without end. A variant, propensity probability, treats it instead as a tendency of the experiment to give that outcome, even if you run it just once.

paragraphs.heading: Probability as belief
paragraphs.text: The other school, the subjectivists, treats a probability as a degree of belief. One way to pin that down is as the price you would pay or accept for a bet that pays 1 unit if the event happens and nothing if it does not. Not everyone accepts that reading. The best-known subjective form is Bayesian probability, which combines expert knowledge with experimental data.

paragraphs.heading: Updating with evidence
paragraphs.text: In the Bayesian view, what experts know at the start is written as a prior, a probability distribution held before the data come in. The data enter through a likelihood function. Multiply the prior and the likelihood, rescale the result, and you get the posterior: a distribution that holds all the information known so far.

paragraphs.heading: When people disagree
paragraphs.text: Two people who reason this way and start from similar priors will end up with similar posteriors. But if their priors are different enough, they can reach different conclusions. That stays true no matter how much information they share.
